system.name: Kepler-90
system.description: The first exosolar system confirmed with eight planets — matching our Solar System's count — 2,545 light-years from Earth.

kepler90-star.name: Kepler-90
kepler90-star.description: Kepler-90 is a Sun-like G-type star located 2,545 light-years from Earth in the constellation Draco. It is notable for hosting eight confirmed planets, tying our Solar System for the most planets known around any star.
kepler90-star.funFact: The eighth planet Kepler-90i was discovered in 2017 using Google's machine learning neural network applied to Kepler data.

kepler90-b.name: Kepler-90 b
kepler90-b.description: Kepler-90 b is the innermost known planet of the Kepler-90 system, orbiting very close to the star with a period of just over 7 days. It is classified as a super-Earth or mini-Neptune, substantially larger than Earth.
kepler90-b.funFact: Kepler-90 b was discovered by NASA's Kepler space telescope through the transit method, detecting the tiny dip in starlight as the planet passed in front of its star.

kepler90-c.name: Kepler-90 c
kepler90-c.description: Kepler-90 c is the second planet from the star and has a similar size to its inner neighbor. It orbits in near-resonance with several other planets in the system, suggesting gravitational interactions shaped its orbit.
kepler90-c.funFact: The compact architecture of the inner Kepler-90 planets resembles a scaled-up version of our Solar System's inner planets packed into a much smaller space.

kepler90-i.name: Kepler-90 i
kepler90-i.description: Kepler-90 i was the eighth planet discovered in the system and the one found by Google's AI. It occupies the third orbital slot and is roughly 1.32 times the size of Earth, receiving intense radiation from its nearby star.
kepler90-i.funFact: Kepler-90 i was identified by an AI trained on 15,000 Kepler signals, demonstrating how machine learning can find planets humans might miss.

kepler90-d.name: Kepler-90 d
kepler90-d.description: Kepler-90 d is a sub-Neptune class planet significantly larger than Earth. It sits further out in the system where the star's radiation is less intense, and may have a thick hydrogen-helium envelope surrounding a rocky or icy core.
kepler90-d.funFact: The jump in size from the inner rocky planets to Kepler-90 d mirrors the transition from the inner to outer planets in our own Solar System.

kepler90-e.name: Kepler-90 e
kepler90-e.description: Kepler-90 e is another sub-Neptune in the system's middle region. With a radius about 2.67 times Earth's, it falls into the category of planets with no Solar System analog — intermediate between rocky super-Earths and ice giants.
kepler90-e.funFact: Kepler-90 e's mass and radius suggest it has a rocky core surrounded by a substantial volatile envelope, possibly including water ice.

kepler90-f.name: Kepler-90 f
kepler90-f.description: Kepler-90 f is the outermost of the sub-Neptune planets in the system. It has a similar size to Kepler-90 d but orbits much further out, placing it in a region where temperatures would allow water ice to be stable.
kepler90-f.funFact: Kepler-90 f's orbital period of about 125 days is remarkably close to Venus's 225-day period scaled to the Kepler-90 system's size.

kepler90-g.name: Kepler-90 g
kepler90-g.description: Kepler-90 g is the larger of two gas giant planets in the system, with a radius about 8.1 times that of Earth — placing it in Jupiter's size class. It orbits in the system's outer region, completing one orbit every 210 days.
kepler90-g.funFact: The presence of two large gas giants in the outer Kepler-90 system and several smaller planets in the inner system is strikingly similar to the architecture of our Solar System.

kepler90-h.name: Kepler-90 h
kepler90-h.description: Kepler-90 h is the outermost known planet in the Kepler-90 system and the largest, with a radius about 11.3 times Earth's — comparable to Saturn. It takes about 332 days to complete one orbit, nearly matching Earth's year.
kepler90-h.funFact: Kepler-90 h's discovery made Kepler-90 the first exostar known to host as many planets as our Solar System — eight.
